summary: Discusses how to create NACK-oriented reliable multicast protocols. It explains the goals and assumptions, identifies technical challenges, and breaks them into functional building blocks. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5401.

eli5.summary: It is the box of parts and the design notes for building a reliable one-to-many delivery system, rather than the finished system.

subtitle: Design components for reliable multicast using negative acknowledgments.

tldr.problem: IP multicast can reach large groups efficiently, but delivering data reliably to all receivers is hard. Standard acknowledgment schemes do not scale to large groups.
tldr.mechanism: NORM (Negative-Acknowledgment-Oriented Reliable Multicast) provides building blocks where receivers send repair requests only for lost packets, rather than acknowledging every reception. Probabilistic suppression of these requests scales to tens of thousands of receivers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was experimental and has been replaced by RFC 5401, which consolidates the specification into a complete protocol definition.

today: RFC 3941 is an Experimental specification that has been superseded by RFC 5401, which consolidates the specification into a complete protocol definition with additional clarifications and fixes.

sections.title: Introduction to NORM
sections.content:
NORM stands for Negative-Acknowledgment-Oriented Reliable Multicast. This RFC lays out the design building blocks and rationale for protocols that guarantee reliable delivery to multicast groups by having receivers request repairs only when they detect loss, rather than sending acknowledgments for successful receipt.

The document is part of the IETF Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) working group effort. It focuses on three areas not addressed in other building block documents: sender transmission strategies, the NACK-oriented repair process with timer-based feedback suppression, and round-trip timing (RTT) for adapting protocol timers. It is experimental and awaited congestion control integration before standardization.
sections.eli5: NORM is the blueprint for a multicast system where receivers only complain when something arrives broken, rather than confirming every arrival.

sections.title: Design Goals and Assumptions
sections.content: NORM building blocks address several key design areas. Delivery service model: protocols target bulk data transfer, though the design can serve interactive messaging. Group membership dynamics: receivers may join late, leave, and rejoin while a session stays active. Sender/receiver relationships: the protocol supports one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many scenarios. Group size scalability: research suggests NACK-based protocols can handle tens of thousands of receivers with modest feedback. Data delivery performance: there is a trade-off between scalability (which requires delays for NACK suppression) and latency. Network environments: the protocol must work across heterogeneous networks from wireless links to high-speed LANs, including asymmetric topologies where only single-source multicast is available. Router assistance: while the protocol works without intermediate help, it can benefit from NACK aggregation at routers when available.
sections.eli5: The protocol must handle groups of any size, networks of any speed, and let people join or leave without breaking everything.

sections.title: Sender Transmission and NACK Process
sections.content:
A NORM sender transmits data content at a rate controlled by congestion control and application requirements. The sender may interleave new data transmission with repair packets in response to receiver NACKs. The sender advertises its current Group Round-Trip Time (GRTT) estimate to the group, which receivers use to set their NACK suppression timers.

When a receiver detects missing packets, it initiates a NACK cycle by setting a backoff timeout chosen randomly from a truncated exponential distribution. The mean of this distribution is determined by the group size estimate and the sender's advertised GRTT. This probabilistic approach ensures that only a small fraction of receivers send NACKs, even when all need repair. When the backoff expires, a receiver transmits a NACK only if its repair needs have not been satisfied by NACKs heard from other receivers or by observing the sender's transmission progress. The sender waits for a period equal to the maximum receiver backoff time plus RTT propagation delay before responding to accumulated NACKs, allowing it to aggregate multiple repair requests efficiently.
sections.eli5: When packets go missing, receivers wait a random amount of time before asking for replacements. If someone else already asked, they stay quiet. The sender listens to all the requests before sending fixes.

sections.title: FEC and Repair Content
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) encodes data into parity packets, allowing receivers to reconstruct missing data without requesting retransmission. When FEC is used, a receiver's NACK content can indicate how many packets it is missing within a coding block, and the sender responds with new, previously untransmitted parity packets. If an FEC code permits (as Reed-Solomon codes do), receivers can explicitly request the specific parity symbols they need, allowing fine-grained repair and better suppression across the group.

NACK content is organized hierarchically: a session contains senders, each sender contains objects or streams, each object contains FEC blocks, and each block contains symbols. NACK messages identify missing symbols by their object, block, and symbol indices. This hierarchical structure allows a single NACK to request repair for multiple blocks or even an entire object if necessary.
sections.eli5: With error correction, a receiver can say "I need parity packets 5 through 7" instead of "please retransmit packets 2, 5, and 8." It's more efficient.

sections.title: Measuring Network Timing
sections.content:
The sender periodically sends probe messages with a timestamp. Receivers record the send time and the time they receive it, then echo back a response. The sender measures the round-trip time (RTT) from each receiver and maintains the peak RTT seen (GRTT), capped at 90% of the previous estimate plus any new peak. The GRTT estimate is quantized to a single byte and advertised in all sender messages. This allows the sender and receivers to synchronize their timer-based operations without requiring clock synchronization.

Receivers may also measure RTT independently and report it back using suppression techniques similar to NACK suppression, avoiding feedback overload. For protocols with multiple senders, receivers can estimate RTT to a new sender using known RTTs between group members via the triangle inequality.
sections.eli5: The sender regularly asks "can you hear me?" and records how long replies take. It then tells everyone the worst-case delay so they can time their requests properly.

sections.title: Security and Operational Concerns
sections.content: NORM protocols are subject to the same vulnerabilities as IP and IP multicast. IPsec authentication is recommended for protection against session intrusion and denial-of-service attacks. A particular threat for NACK-based protocols is NACK replay, where an attacker replays old repair requests to prevent the sender from making forward progress. IPsec replay protection is recommended, and NORM protocol instantiations may provide their own replay protection if network-layer mechanisms are unavailable. Buffering requirements for NORM are greater than for point-to-point reliable protocols like TCP because of the disparity in receiver connectivity and the feedback delays required for scalability. Applications must understand the latency/scalability trade-off when setting maximum backoff timeout values.
sections.eli5: An attacker could trick the sender into wasting time fixing things that already got fixed, or pretend to be many receivers to ask for lots of repairs at once. Encryption and authentication help prevent these attacks.
